title: The Prince
author: Niccolo Machiavelli
teaches: that power is won by appearing one thing and being another, and that the appearance is the thing most people actually judge you by.
fruit: the Prince tells you to ask what a ruler's fear and favour produce on the ground, not what his virtue is declared to be; a real authority leaves ends behind it.

title: Following the Equator: A Journey Around the World
author: Mark Twain
teaches: how a practised confidence man talks a mark out of his money, and how the mark's own vanity and self-flattery do half the work.
fruit: the mark is always the one who is impressed; Twain shows you the mark's side of the table so you can watch yourself being worked.

title: Propaganda
author: Edward L. Bernays
teaches: the eight standard methods of public opinion, named by the man who named propaganda itself, so the move can be seen rather than felt.
fruit: Bernays's eight methods make the agenda legible: a text using testimonial, social class, and prestige is doing the thing, whether it admits it or not.

title: Crystallizing Public Opinion
author: Edward L. Bernays
teaches: how opinion is organised and crystallised before it is ever held, so that a reaction can be presented as a spontaneous public judgement.
fruit: it distinguishes opinion that was organised from opinion that was merely expressed, which is the difference between a real consensus and a manufactured one.

title: News from Nowhere; Or, An Epoch of Rest
author: William Morris
teaches: what a world without wage-slavery and without the false needs that justify it would look like, which lets you see the false need in outline.
fruit: it supplies the honest alternative; anything that survives comparison with this is a want you actually chose, and anything that vanishes is a manufactured one.

title: The History of Don Quixote
author: Miguel de Cervantes
teaches: how a madman reads the world as a conspiracy of enchanters when it is only the ordinary world failing to behave as belief expects.
fruit: the sane characters keep insisting the world is as it is; a reader who keeps checking the reality of the claim is doing what the squire does.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
teaches: the Grand Inquisitor's argument that a humanity which cannot bear freedom will hand its freedom to an authority that promises bread and safety.
fruit: the Grand Inquisitor offers the reader the exact terms of the bargain, so you can hear whether the offer in front of you makes the same one.

title: Moby-Dick; or, The Whale
author: Herman Melville
teaches: Ahab's speech against the false idols of what men agree to worship, which is the speech of the man who has already been consumed by them.
fruit: Ahab shows what happens when a person treats an agreed story as the real thing; the reader can check whether the idol in front of them survives contact with reality.

title: The Confidence-Man: His Masquerade
author: Herman Melville
teaches: the confidence man in every disguise, from the sociable to the fraudulent, working a whole ship of believers who each supply their own reasons to believe.
fruit: the mark is never deceived by cleverness alone; Melville shows the mark's own wish to be deceived, which is the tell a con artist cannot cover.

title: The Charterhouse of Parma
author: Stendhal
teaches: Count Mosca's great con, the marriage of a kept woman to a real count that manufactures a title out of nothing and lets the court believe it.
fruit: Mosca's success depends on the court wanting to believe the title, so the reader learns to ask who profits from my credulity and who supplied it.

title: Lord Jim
author: Joseph Conrad
teaches: the man who is not a criminal, whose one lapse makes him refuse to be one thing or the other, and so is condemned by both.
fruit: Jim's case separates the act from the man, so a reader can tell a real lapse of judgment from an identity that was performed all along.

title: The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
teaches: the split, where a public reputation and a private one are kept apart until the private one walks out wearing the public one's clothes.
fruit: the text tracks what each transformation costs the man who makes it, which is the question to ask of any self that is presented as two-faced.

title: A Tale of a Tub
author: Jonathan Swift
teaches: how the same clothes, the same doctrines and the same borrowed names are made to do opposite work, so that a reader's own words are turned against him.
fruit: Swift shows that a borrowed label can be silently swapped for its opposite, so a reader can test whether a name still fits what it names.

title: The Count of Monte Cristo
author: Alexandre Dumas
teaches: the great con at scale, a returned man who builds an identity out of borrowed wealth and lets a society confirm the story because it profits from it.
fruit: Monte Cristo works because every accomplice has a reason to maintain the fiction; the reader learns to look for who benefits from my belief, not who seems credible.

title: The Idiot
author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
teaches: what happens to a person who refuses to calculate, in a society where every transaction is calculated.
fruit: the book separates the man who believes everyone from the man who has been taken in, which is a different kind of failure entirely.

title: Courts, Criminals, and the Camorra
author: Arthur Cheney Train
teaches: an organised criminal society's relation to the courts it pays and corrupts, and the machinery that keeps its authority unquestioned.
fruit: Train shows the point at which a criminal order and a legal one become indistinguishable, so the reader can find the seam where a real authority is bought.

title: The Sicilian Bandit
author: Alexandre Dumas
teaches: the Sicilian bandit as a figure of protection and justice, which is how a robber becomes the community's own idea of law.
fruit: the bandit is trusted because the community wants him trusted, so the reader can ask whether the protection in front of them was ever bought or earned.

title: Brigands of the Moon
author: Ray Cummings
teaches: robbery organised as a business with a hierarchy, a product and a distribution system.
fruit: the text treats the band as a firm with costs and logistics, so the reader can read a protection racket as a business rather than as fear.

title: Among the Brigands
author: James de Mille
teaches: the brigand from inside a country where his power is the law the villagers actually live under.
fruit: the text shows the band and the state as two rival authorities, and the reader can see which one the villagers actually obey.

title: Corse de Leon; or, The Brigand
author: G. P. R. James
teaches: the romantic brigand whose legend outgrows the man, so the reputation outlives the deeds.
fruit: James shows reputation replacing evidence, which is exactly the ground a reader stands on when judging a name they have only heard.

title: Sketches of Imposture, Deception, and Credulity
author: Richard Alfred Davenport
teaches: a catalogue of specific impostures worked out one by one, with the credulity that each one was built to meet.
fruit: each case pairs the trick with the want it fed on, so the reader can recognise the appetite rather than only the method.

title: The Humbugs of the World: An Account of Humbugs, Delusions, Impostures, and Chimneys
author: P. T. Barnum
teaches: the showman on his own trade, naming the humbugs he sold and how each one was made to look like what the buyer wanted.
fruit: Barnum confesses which of his shows were fakes and which were not, which is the test the reader can apply to any claim of wonder.

title: Struggles and Triumphs; or, Forty Years' Recollections of P. T. Barnum
author: P. T. Barnum
teaches: the con artist in autobiography, including the failures and the frauds that nearly finished him, told by the man who ran them.
fruit: the record includes the failures, which is exactly what a real one does and what advertising never does.

title: The Autobiography of a Quack, and The Case of George Dedlow
author: S. Weir Mitchell
teaches: a quack physician on his own practice, and the ordinary social machinery that lets a false authority keep its position.
fruit: the quack's position depends on the community that protects him, so the reader can look at the institution rather than only the man.

title: Quacks and Grafters
author: George R. Strain (ex-osteopath)
teaches: an expose of the healing trade's false practitioners and the profit that keeps them in business.
fruit: the text names who benefits from the false cure, so the reader can check whether the treatment's author or its buyer is profiting.

title: The Great American Fraud
author: Samuel Hopkins Adams
teaches: the patent medicine industry's whole method of manufacture, from the testimonial to the analysable bottle, itemised.
fruit: the fundamental fakes are listed by name, so the reader can take a bottle or a claim apart and find the specific device in it.

title: Counterfeit Money: The 'Green Goods' Business Exposed
author: Anonymous
teaches: the counterfeit-note trade from inside, written to be read by the people running it, which is why it names every step.
fruit: the text shows what the trade needs from the person it deceives, so the reader can spot the demand that makes a fraud workable.

title: The Man That Corrupted Hadleyburg
author: Mark Twain
teaches: how a whole honest town is bought with a piece of paper, and how the buying makes the town complicit in its own deception.
fruit: Hadleyburg shows that credibility is collectively manufactured, so the reader can ask who the town and the man each needed to believe.

title: A Burlesque Autobiography
author: Mark Twain
teaches: Twain's account of his own brush with the Confidence-Man and his adoption of the swindler's craft of telling the truth so plausibly it becomes a lie.
fruit: Twain tells the swindler's story in the swindler's voice, so the reader can recognise the technique in a flattering account of themselves.

title: The Prince and the Pauper
author: Mark Twain
teaches: a prince and a pauper who each wear the other's clothes and are mistaken for each other, so rank is shown to be a costume rather than a person.
fruit: the swap proves that rank is read off dress and bearing, so the reader can check what in a claimed authority is the person and what is the costume.

title: The Magician's Own Book, or, The Whole Art of Conjuring
author: George Arnold
teaches: the conjurer's working method, including the misdirection and the confederate, described by a working magician.
fruit: the book gives the mechanisms, so a reader can look for the hand behind the wonder instead of the wonder itself.

title: The Alchemist
author: Ben Jonson
teaches: the alchemist's house as a con operation, where the fake gold and the false prophecy are made to pay for the household.
fruit: Face and Subtle both profit from the same lie, so the reader can see that a deception which pays everyone involved is the hardest kind to check.

title: Volpone; or, The Fox
author: Ben Jonson
teaches: the legacy-hunter who courts the dying for their wills and turns inheritance into a staged performance of virtue.
fruit: Volpone's performance depends on each listener wanting the estate, so the reader can spot the shared interest behind the flattery.

title: A Treatise on Relics
author: John Calvin
teaches: how relics and pilgrimage are manufactured and traded as contact with the holy, and how the fraud is detected by checking the claim itself.
fruit: Calvin's test is documentary, so the reader can learn to ask what the record says rather than how moving the object feels.

title: The Three Impostors
author: Arthur Machen
teaches: imposture at the level of identity, where the false is not a falsehood but a substitution of one person for another.
fruit: the three impostors are indistinguishable by their own account of themselves, which teaches the reader to test a claim against more than one source.

title: The History of Caliph Vathek
author: William Beckford
teaches: the ruler who trades his soul for power and learns that the bargain was always a swindle, since the thing he bought was never real.
fruit: Vathek's transaction fails on inspection, so the reader can check whether what a claim buys is actually delivered.

title: Our Friend the Charlatan
author: George Gissing
teaches: the intellectual who runs a fake society and teaches a doctrine of his own devising while appearing to serve a cause.
fruit: the charlatan is exposed by what he takes and what he avoids paying, so the reader can test a doctrine by following its author's money.

title: Tartuffe; or, The Hypocrite
author: Molière
teaches: the holy man who takes a household apart by pretending to serve it, and whose fraud is protected by the reputation he has built.
fruit: Tartuffe's protection is the reputation, so the reader can ask what would remain if the reputation were removed.

title: The Gulistan (Rose Garden) of Sa'di
author: Sa'di
teaches: the Persian master on the difference between the appearance of a life and the life, and on how the world deceives those who serve it.
fruit: Sa'di asks whether the thing that was gained can be spent and whether what was learned can be used, which separates a real master from an admired one.

title: The Bustan of Sa'di
author: Sa'di
teaches: the master's garden of moral teaching, on the uses of knowledge and the harm of knowledge kept for show.
fruit: the Bustan tests teaching by its effect on conduct, so the reader can ask what a claim to knowledge changed in the claimant.

title: The Sufism of the Rubaiyat; or, The Secret of the Great Paradox
author: Omar Khayyam / Norton F. W. Hazeldine
teaches: the paradox that the veils and the wine are one thing, and that the apparent contradiction resolves at a level the sensual eye cannot reach.
fruit: the paradox is only resolvable by the one who has crossed, so the reader can distinguish a claim to have crossed from a claim to know about it.

title: The Sufistic Quatrains of Omar Khayyam
author: Omar Khayyam
teaches: the quatrain read as a Sufi document, where the wine and the beloved are the veil on the beloved of the soul.
fruit: it gives a second reading under the surface reading, so the reader can ask which level of a statement is being addressed.

title: Persian Literature, Volume 1: The Shah Nameh
author: Firdawsi
teaches: the Persian epic of the king who is given what he wants and loses everything by it, the fable of power under a different name.
fruit: the Shah Nameh shows the cost of what is granted, so the reader can price a gift that comes with nothing attached.

title: The Zincali: An Account of the Gypsies of Spain
author: George Borrow
teaches: the Roma people observed from inside their own society, including the practices the settled world calls trickery.
fruit: Borrow's account is written by an outsider who admits the frame, so the reader can weigh the description against the judgement.

title: Master Reynard: The History of a Fox
author: Jane Fielding / John G. Tregarthen
teaches: the animal-trickster tradition of Reynard the Fox, in which every swindle is a piece of rhetoric and the victim collaborates.
fruit: Reynard's jokes are won by flattering the mark, so the reader can recognise the flattery in a swindle addressed to them.

title: The Decameron
author: Giovanni Boccaccio
teaches: the ten young people who tell each other stories of fraud and appetite, and the framing itself a way of passing on what cannot be said directly.
fruit: each tale is told by a named character with a motive, so the reader can ask who is profiting from the account being told.

title: The Slang Dictionary
author: John Camden Hotten
teaches: the working vocabulary of the fraud trade and the streets it operates on, with dates and first uses.
fruit: a word's first use and date are a record of a practice, so the reader can tell when a scheme was invented and how old it is.

title: Telepathy, Genuine and Fraudulent
author: W. W. Baggally
teaches: the examiner's own effort to separate what was transmitted from what was produced by the operator, with the fraudulent cases itemised.
fruit: the book asks whether anything actually transferred, so a reader can ask that question of any claim of second sight or remote influence.

title: Fables in Slang
author: George Ade
teaches: short vernacular fables of the sharp and the mark, told in the idiom the trade actually speaks.
fruit: the fables are short enough to check against a real case, so the reader can test a story against the pattern it fits.
